title: Lymph node metastasis mapping after neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy in gastric and gastroesophageal junction cancer: A pooled analysis of 4 prospective clinical trials
abstract: Although neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy (NICT) has improved survival in locally advanced gastric cancer (GC) and gastroesophageal junction cancer (GEJC), lymph node metastasis (LNM) patterns following NICT remain undefined. We aimed to characterize topographical LNM patterns after NICT and evaluate the association between lymphadenectomy extent, surgical approach, and survival outcomes. Data were pooled from 4 prospective clinical trials (NEOSUMMIT-01 - 04), comprising 126 patients with GC (n = 61) or GEJC (n = 65) undergoing curative gastrectomy following NICT. ypN0 was achieved in 71 patients (56%). In GEJC, station No. 3, 7 were high risk; No. 1, 2, 9, and 11 were intermediate risk; and No. 4, 5, 6, 8, 12 were low risk. In GC, station No. 12 was low-risk; D1 stations (No. 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7) were high-risk, D1+ stations (No. 8, 9) and No. 11 were intermediate-risk. At a median follow-up of 36.2 months, 24-month EFS and OS rates were 76.4% and 90.5%. Nodal yield (≥30 vs. < 30) was not significantly associated with EFS (P = .611) or OS (P = .911). In exploratory comparisons within the GEJC cohort, EFS (P = .219) and OS (P = .290) did not differ significantly between proximal and total gastrectomy. In GEJC, distal perigastric lymph node stations (No. 4, 5, 6, and 12) exhibited low metastasis rates, while exploratory survival outcomes support prospective clinical trials of proximal gastrectomy in appropriately selected patients. Conversely, the broader residual nodal involvement in GC reinforces the continued role of standard D2 lymphadenectomy.

title: Acute MCL1 loss via homoharringtonine-mediated translational inhibition enables potent apoptotic synergy with BCLXL blockade
abstract: Antiapoptotic buffering in solid tumors is generally mediated by both BCLXL and MCL1, so that BH3 mimetic drugs targeting only one have limited efficacy. To identify agents that may sensitize tumors to BH3 mimetics targeting BCLXL, we screened prostate cancer cells against a panel of mitochondria-targeted drugs in combination with navitoclax, a BH3 mimetic targeting BCL2 and BCLXL. Homoharringtonine (HHT) in combination with navitoclax and as a single agent emerged as a potent inducer of apoptosis. HHT has been identified as an inhibitor of protein translation, and proteomic analysis showed broad suppression of translation-related pathways, while immunoblotting demonstrated rapid decreases in short-lived proteins, including MCL1. HHT dose response and time course studies showed marked declines in MCL1 within 2 h that were associated with apoptosis in response to BCLXL inhibition with navitoclax or A1331852. Further cell viability assays showed synergy between HHT and BCLXL inhibitors in multiple prostate, lung, and colorectal cancer cell lines. HHT monotherapy in vivo caused tumor regression in two prostate cancer xenograft models. Analysis of tumor tissue taken at 4 h after dosing showed decreases in MCL1 and MYC, indicating that HHT levels obtainable in vivo are adequate to deplete short-lived proteins and potentially sensitize to BH3 mimetics targeting BCLXL. These findings support further exploration of HHT as a single agent in solid tumors and establish a rationale for investigating safer, tumor-selective approaches to combine HHT-mediated translational inhibition with BCLXL targeting.

title: Therapy-associated myeloid niches as spatial drivers of cancer treatment resistance and targets for mechanism-matched intervention
abstract: Tumor drug resistance is still the core obstacle limiting the long-term benefit of modern anticancer therapy, especially in the context of treatment tolerance, persistence of minimal residual disease (MRD) and recurrence after treatment. Increasing evidence has shown that therapy-associated myeloid niches can involve cell recruitment, enrichment of pre-existing populations, or state reprogramming, together with local relationships among myeloid cells, tumor cells, stroma, vessels, and other immune cells. These niches can support residual tumor-cell survival, immune escape, local regrowth, and distant dissemination through overlapping mechanisms linking fibrotic exclusion and perivascular organization with hypoxic metabolic suppression and myeloid replenishment. The formation of neutrophil extracellular traps, failure of antigen uptake and presentation, impaired T-cell priming, and phagocytic escape can further sustain treatment tolerance. Focusing on the myeloid cell state and common molecular circuits, this article presents an evidence assessment framework that interprets spatial and clinical associations alongside functional and pharmacologic findings without assigning hierarchical ranks. It summarizes lessons from clinical failure, considering potentially limited target contributions, compensatory pathways, inadequate exposure, and toxicity, while distinguishing drug exposure and local pharmacodynamic changes from clinical benefit. Candidate biomarkers, intervention windows, and selective delivery approaches require validation to guide mechanism-matched combinations. In the future, longitudinal tissue analyses, functional validation, and prospective studies should test whether these combinations provide durable benefit with acceptable safety in defined patient populations and treatment settings.

title: SPP1+ TAMs drive colorectal tumorigenesis through an ARG2-orchestrated metabolic-immune crosstalk
abstract: Rising incidence of colorectal cancer (CRC) and limited therapeutic options highlight the urgent need to define the drivers of its progression. The SPP1 + tumor-associated macrophage (TAM) subset identified by single-cell transcriptomics is a functionally dominant population that extends beyond the classical M1/M2 paradigm. Here, we dissected the molecular mechanisms by which SPP1 + TAMs reprogram tumor progression and determined whether the gut microbiota regulates this process in colorectal cancer. Using a multi-platform strategy integrating clinical specimens, murine models and CRC cell lines, we found that SPP1 + TAMs increase progressively during CRC evolution and exhibit crosstalk with malignant epithelial cells, and their abundance is associated with adverse clinical outcome. Integrative analysis reveals a significant positive correlation between SPP1 and ARG2 expression. Further, TAM-derived SPP1 engages CD44 on CRC cells to induce ARG2 expression. Mechanistically, ARG2 facilitates the interaction between USP10 and c-Myc to deubiquitinate and stabilize c-Myc, which transactivates the glycolytic enzyme HK2, driving Warburg metabolism that fuels CRC cell proliferation. Moreover, ARG2 secreted by CRC cells is internalized by TAMs, which reciprocally upregulates SPP1, creating a feed-forward loop that drives a pro-tumorigenic microenvironment. Notably, Bifidobacterium longum downregulates CD44 expression on tumor cells, thereby disrupting the SPP1-ARG2 axis and attenuating CRC progression. These findings identify the SPP1-ARG2 circuit as a therapeutic target and propose B. longum as a microbiome-derived precision adjuvant therapy for CRC suppression.

title: Extracellular vesicle-associated LMP1 from EBV-positive nasopharyngeal carcinoma induces LIF-mediated immunosuppressive macrophage polarization and impairs anti-tumor immunity
abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-associated nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is characterized by a highly infiltrated yet immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), in which tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) contribute to disease progression. Here, we identify an extracellular vesicle (EV)-mediated LMP1-NF-κB-LIF signaling axis that promotes macrophage reprogramming and immune suppression in NPC. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis revealed that EV exposure induces transcriptional remodeling across tumor and immune-cell populations, accompanied by an increased proportion of TAMs within the myeloid compartment. NPC-derived EVs were taken up by macrophages, where EV-associated LMP1 induced NF-κB activation, LIF expression, and polarization toward an immunosuppressive phenotype. Loss- and gain-of-function studies, together with structure-function analyses of the LMP1 CTAR1/CTAR2 domains, further supported the requirement of these CTAR domains for efficient NF-κB activation and LIF induction. Functionally, EV-educated macrophages exhibited impaired phagocytic activity and promoted inhibitory T-cell responses. In zebrafish, 3D spheroid, and mouse xenograft models, EV-educated macrophages promoted NPC growth and vascular dissemination, whereas blockade of LIF signaling with soluble LIFR attenuated these effects. Tumor LIF expression positively correlated with CTLA4 expression. In NPC tissues, LIF expression was preferentially associated with stromal macrophages, and elevated stromal LIF expression was associated with metastasis, advanced nodal disease, and advanced clinical stage. Stromal immune-cell LMP1 expression also correlated with LIF expression and was higher in patients who developed metastasis. Collectively, these findings support an EV-associated LMP1-NF-κB-LIF axis that links EBV-positive NPC cells to macrophage-mediated immune suppression and tumor progression and provide a basis for further investigating this pathway as a potential therapeutic target.

title: A self-amplifying IL-1β–CCL2 circuit between macrophages and cancer-associated fibroblasts drives colorectal cancer progression
abstract: Reciprocal interactions between immune and stromal cells are increasingly recognized as major determinants of colorectal cancer (CRC) progression. However, the specific macrophage and fibroblast states cooperating to establish and sustain a tumor-promoting microenvironment remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify a self-reinforcing inflammatory circuit linking monocyte-derived IL-1β + macrophages with IL1R1 + cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) in CRC. Integrated single-cell transcriptomic analyses of human CRC revealed a marked expansion of IL1B-associated inflammatory macrophages and IL1R1 + inflammatory CAFs, with their respective and combined transcriptional signatures associated with adverse clinical outcomes. Pseudotime analysis and Ms4a3 lineage tracing supported a predominantly monocyte-derived origin of IL-1β + macrophages in the tumor microenvironment. Mechanistically, macrophage-derived IL-1β activated IL1R1 signaling in fibroblasts, promoting the acquisition and expansion of an inflammatory CAF state. Myeloid Il1b deletion or fibroblast-lineage Il1r1 deletion disrupted this interaction and suppressed tumor growth in vivo. In turn, IL1R1 + CAFs produced abundant CCL2, which recruited CCR2 + monocytes and replenished the IL-1β + macrophage population. Fibroblast-lineage Ccl2 deletion, myeloid Ccr2 deletion, and CCL2 rescue experiments established the functional requirement of the CCL2-CCR2 axis for closure of this reciprocal circuit. Acquisition of the IL-1β + inflammatory macrophage program was further supported by coordinated NF-κB and AP-1 activity, with RELA and JUN/FOS contributing to IL1B transcriptional regulation. Finally, therapeutic blockade of either IL-1β or CCL2 disrupted the macrophage-CAF circuit, increased intratumoral CD8 + T-cell responses, and enhanced the antitumor efficacy of anti-PD-1 therapy. Collectively, our findings establish the IL-1β-IL1R1-CCL2-CCR2 axis as a self-amplifying immune-stromal circuit that sustains a tumor-promoting and immunosuppressive microenvironment in CRC. By demonstrating that disruption of this circuit restores antitumor immune activity and sensitizes tumors to PD-1 blockade, our study provides a mechanistic and preclinical rationale for targeting IL-1β-CCL2-mediated macrophage-CAF crosstalk as a combination strategy to improve immunotherapy responses in CRC.

title: MDK+ cancer-associated fibroblasts promote immunotherapy resistance through mitochondrial reprogramming in breast cancer
abstract: Immunotherapy has improved outcomes for patients with breast cancer, yet therapeutic resistance remains a major clinical challenge. Therefore, we integrated single-cell and spatial transcriptomic data from breast cancer cohorts treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors to identify resistance-associated cellular populations and pathways, with validation across five independent bulk RNA-seq immunotherapy cohorts. Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) were isolated from anti-PD-1-resistant breast tumors for functional studies, including in vitro co-culture and in vivo models. Mitochondrial function and metabolic alterations were assessed by flow cytometry, transmission electron microscopy, ATP and adenosine quantification, and JC-1 staining. Tumor mitochondrial metabolism was markedly upregulated in anti-PD-1 non-responders and consistently associated with poor therapeutic response across validation cohorts. MDK-expressing CAFs were enriched in resistant tumors, exhibited strong interactions with tumor cells, and were negatively associated with intratumoral CD8 + T cell infiltration. Single-cell source contribution and depletion analyses identified CAF-derived MDK as the major paracrine mediator linking stromal signaling to tumor metabolic adaptation and immune suppression. Mechanistically, MDK activated SDC1-dependent PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling in cancer cells, promoting mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming, ATP production, and CD39/CD73-dependent extracellular adenosine accumulation, thereby suppressing CD8 + T cell cytotoxicity. Receptor-depletion experiments further identified SDC1 as the principal functional receptor mediating these effects. Importantly, CAF-specific MDK depletion or pharmacological MDK inhibition enhanced anti-PD-1 efficacy and restored CD8 + T cell effector activity in vivo. Collectively, MDK + CAFs facilitate anti-PD-1 resistance via mitochondrial rewiring and adenosine-mediated immunosuppression, supporting the MDK-SDC1 axis as a potential therapeutic target for overcoming resistance and improving immunotherapy efficacy in breast cancer.

title: Repurposing antimalarial drug atovaquone in combination with radiation and PD-L1 checkpoint blockade to enhance antitumour response in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC)
abstract: Atovaquone is an approved antimalarial drug which could sensitise tumours to radiation and may modulate tumour immune microenvironment. Here we evaluated the triple combination of radiation with atovaquone plus anti-PD-L1 in HNSCC syngeneic mouse tumour models. We observed significant tumour growth delay induced by the triple combination treatment with differential responses in three different mouse models. There was complete tumour eradication in 6 of 12 mice in the MOCL1 model but not in the other two murine models. The triple combination was associated with increased populations of CD8 + -T Granzyme B+ cells as well as decreased populations of Tregs, CD11b + Gr1 + granulocytic MDSCs and CD11b + Ly.6G + neutrophils. Atovaquone inhibited EGFR and its downstream signalling as well as reduced PD-L1 expression. The differential antitumour effects of the triple combination may be due to different basal and post-treatment levels of PD-L1, pERK1/2 and pS6, in particular, their levels were reduced by atovaquone +/- RT in MOCL1 models and not in the other two murine models. Radiotherapy plus atovaquone combination increased cell cycle arrest in G2/M phase, which led to inhibition of DNA damage repair by homologous recombination and increased cell death. We also observed increased activation of CD8 + -T cells that led to enhanced killing in our HNSCC patient-derived organoid models treated with the triple combination of radiotherapy and atovaquone plus PD-1/PD-L1 blockade. Overall, our results suggest that the triple combination of radiotherapy and atovaquone plus PD-1/PD-L1 blockade has the potential to increase the efficacy of radiotherapy and/or immunotherapy. Thus, this may provide a rationale to further validate this triple combination of radiotherapy and atovaquone plus PD-1/PD-L1 blockade in clinical trials to improve treatment outcomes.

title: Multidimensional Regulation of Metal Ions in the Tumor Microenvironment and Innovative Strategies for Diagnosis and Therapy
abstract: Metal ions serve as key regulators of the dynamic equilibrium within the tumor microenvironment (TME). In recent years, the TME has emerged as a central regulatory hub for tumor initiation, progression, and metastasis; its complexity has become both a frontier and a major challenge in oncology research. Current therapies are often constrained by immune tolerance, metabolic heterogeneity, and microenvironment-mediated escape mechanisms, necessitating breakthroughs in novel targets and strategies. Metal ions, functioning as enzyme cofactors, signaling molecules, and redox regulators, profoundly affect tumor progression by modulating redox homeostasis, immune responses, and metabolic reprogramming. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in metal ion-mediated regulation of the TME. It focuses on elucidating the multidimensional mechanisms by which metal ions facilitate immunogenic remodeling and metabolic interactions, and prospectively explores innovative metal-ion-based diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. It further highlights the potential of personalized metal metabolomics to advance precision oncology and facilitate the clinical translation of metal ion-based theranostic strategies.

title: Macrophage-derived WNT regulates tumor immune microenvironment to reduce colitis-associated colon cancer
abstract: Prolonged colonic inflammation and ulcerative colitis lead to colon cancer. The rapid growth and treatment-resistant nature of these tumors are primarily influenced by an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, which is led by tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs). However, factors influencing or regulating the immunosuppressive nature of TAMs have not been sufficiently studied. In this manuscript, we use a mouse model of colitis-associated colorectal cancer (CRC) to demonstrate that WNT expression in TAMs regulates their immunosuppressive function by inhibiting Glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK-3β) within the macrophages, possibly through an autofeedback loop. GSK-3β is a positive regulator of PD-1 and PD-L1 expression in macrophages and promotes an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Therefore, GSK-3β inhibition alters the immunosuppressive nature of the immune microenvironment and effectively controls tumor growth. In Csf1r.iCre; Porcn fl/fl mice, the absence of macrophage-derived WNT promotes tumor growth in the model of colitis-associated colon cancer. Absence of macrophage-derived WNT stabilizes GSK-3β in macrophages and promotes an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. We also show that pharmacological inhibition of GSK-3β in a macrophage-specific manner, achieved by systemic delivery of a lipo-GSK3β inhibitor, effectively inhibits tumor growth. Therefore, this manuscript demonstrates for the first time that the macrophage-specific modulation of GSK-3β can be a potential target to treat colitis-associated colon cancer.

title: CRISPR-based interrogation of alternative lengthening of telomeres: mapping dependencies, stress-buffering pathways, and therapeutic vulnerabilities
abstract: Alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) is a telomerase-independent telomere maintenance mechanism that supports the growth of approximately 5-10% of human tumors and represents an attractive but insufficiently explored therapeutic target. CRISPR-based functional genomics has emerged as a powerful approach to systematically interrogate ALT biology and identify genetic dependencies associated with the ALT state. In this Review, we discuss the CRISPR-based strategies applied to ALT, including hypothesis-driven targeted loss-of-function screens, phenotype-driven optical screens, in silico mining of large-scale dependency datasets, and genome-wide screens in ALT-adjacent states. Across these approaches, recurrent dependencies converge on pathways mediating replication stress buffering, DNA repair, and telomere maintenance, including FANCM, SMARCAL1, and SUB1. Collectively, these findings support a model in which ALT-positive cells rely not on a unique ALT-specific factor, but rather on stress-buffering mechanisms that prevent chronic telomeric dysfunction from triggering replication catastrophe and cell death, highlighting these pathways as promising candidates for further therapeutic investigation.

title: Verbascoside inhibits ovarian cancer proliferation via IRAK4-CXCL5 axis-mediated suppression of neutrophil infiltration and neutrophil extracellular trap formation
abstract: The specific mechanisms of verbascoside (VB) in ovarian cancer (OC) remain insufficient. This study aimed to explore the anti-tumor mechanisms of VB in OC, focusing on its ability to modulate the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), particularly through targeting neutrophil infiltration and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs). The anti-tumor and anti-NETosis efficacy of VB was evaluated in vivo using subcutaneous, orthotopic, and pulmonary metastasis mouse models of OC. Microproteomics and bioinformatics analysis identified the direct molecular target of VB and the key neutrophil chemoattractant. The underlying mechanisms were validated in vitro and in vivo (using SKOV3, ID8, and neutrophils), alongside loss-of-function approaches. The combination of VB with anti-PD-1 immunotherapy was also assessed. VB inhibited OC proliferation/metastasis, promoted anti-tumor immunity, and suppressed neutrophil infiltration and NETosis. Neutrophil depletion attenuated VB's anti-metastatic effect. Microproteomics and bioinformatics screening identified IRAK4 as a direct molecular target of VB and CXCL5 as a key neutrophil chemoattractant. SPR confirmed the direct binding between VB and IRAK4, and molecular docking revealed specific hydrogen bond interactions. Mechanistically, VB treatment or IRAK4 knockdown suppressed CXCL5 expression, and consequently reduced neutrophil infiltration and NETosis. Consistently, CXCL5 overexpression abrogated the inhibitory effects of VB on neutrophil NETosis and recruitment. Furthermore, VB synergized with anti-PD-1 therapy, thereby achieving superior tumor growth inhibition, reduced Ki67 expression, and enhanced CD8 + T cell infiltration. In conclusion, VB exerts potent anti-tumor effects in OC by targeting the IRAK4/CXCL5 axis, thereby inhibiting neutrophil infiltration and NETosis, reshaping the immunosuppressive TME, and restoring anti-tumor immunity.

title: Profiling circulating tumor DNA for recurrence prediction and prevention in hepatocellular carcinoma following liver transplantation
abstract: Sensitive biomarkers for recurrence risk stratification, recurrence surveillance and adjuvant therapy guidance are of unmet need for patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) undergoing liver transplantation (LT). Herein, we explored the potential of profiling circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) for prediction and prevention of recurrence in HCC after LT. HCC patients (n = 91) who underwent LT were prospectively enrolled. ctDNA was assayed using next-generation sequencing from perioperative plasma (n = 408). Associations between ctDNA status with clinicopathological parameters, tumor recurrence, and adjuvant treatment effect were analyzed. Higher preoperative ctDNA burden correlated with microvascular invasion (median: 45.0 vs 5.1 MTM/mL, P = 0.003) and recurrence (156.2 vs 7.7 MTM/mL, P < 0.001). ctDNA clearance was noted in 87.7% patients after LT and patients who kept positive postoperative ctDNA showed higher recurrence risk (HR = 8.86, P < 0.001), especially early recurrence (within 1 year; 75.0% vs 10.1%, P < 0.001). During follow-up, positive longitudinal ctDNA was similarly predictive of recurrence (HR = 36.50, P < 0.001). The AUC of longitudinal ctDNA for predicting recurrence was 0.930-significantly higher than alpha-fetoprotein (0.655, P < 0.001). Longitudinal ctDNA detected radiologically evidenced recurrence with a median lead time of 5.1 months compared to standard-of-care surveillance. Among patients who received adjuvant therapy, those with positive postoperative ctDNA could benefit (HR = 0.11, P = 0.003) and those with decreased ctDNA burden following treatment experienced longer interval from ctDNA positivity to recurrence (HR = 0.17, P = 0.006). Serial ctDNA analysis demonstrates strong prognostic value, capable of heralding tumor recurrence prior to radiological recurrence and measuring treatment efficacy. Its integration into clinical practice of HCC provides unique opportunities for adjuvant therapy decision-making following LT.

title: 2-Hydroxyisobutyrylation of SRSF9 regulates CD44 alternative splicing to promote colorectal cancer liver metastasis
abstract: Colorectal cancer liver metastasis (CRLM) remains a major cause of cancer mortality, yet the metabolic mechanisms that remodel metastatic RNA-splicing programs are poorly defined. Here, integrated quantitative proteomics and lysine 2-hydroxyisobutyrylation (Khib) proteomics of patient-matched normal mucosa, primary CRCs, and liver metastases revealed a progressive increase in global Khib, with enrichment on RNA-splicing proteins. Serine/arginine-rich splicing factor 9 (SRSF9) emerged as a Khib-modified splicing factor whose expression and K155 Khib levels increased from normal tissue to primary tumors and liver metastases. Gain and loss of function studies in CRC cell lines, patient-derived organoids, subcutaneous xenografts, and splenic injection liver metastasis models showed that SRSF9 promotes proliferation, invasion, tumor growth, and liver colonization. Mechanistically, K155 Khib stabilized SRSF9 protein; the K155R mutation accelerated degradation and abolished SRSF9-driven malignant phenotypes. KAT7 and SIRT6 act as regulators of Khib modification, which positively and negatively modulate the K155 Khib modification of SRSF9, respectively. SRSF9 bound CD44 pre-mRNA through its RRM1 domain and promoted alternative splicing toward the oncogenic CD44V8-10 isoform, which was elevated in patient tumors and metastases and rescued the impaired proliferation and metastatic capacity caused by SRSF9 loss. Finally, a CD44V8-10-targeting antisense oligonucleotide suppressed CRC growth and liver metastasis in preclinical models. These findings define a KAT7/SIRT6-regulated Khib-SRSF9-CD44V8-10 axis that couples metabolic acylation to metastatic splicing and nominate CD44V8-10 as a therapeutic vulnerability in CRC liver metastasis.

title: Tumor-like alterations in brain tissue adjacent to glioblastoma: an integrated analysis based on continuous en bloc resection strategy
abstract: The prognosis for glioblastoma (GBM) is correlated with the extent of resection. Continuous en bloc resection (CEBR) is a surgical strategy that involves the removal of the gross tumor along with its normal adjacent tissue (NAT) as "one whole block". However, its impact on the survival of patients with GBM in non-eloquent areas is unknown. We found that CEBR significantly prolongs both overall survival and progression-free survival in patients with GBM in non-eloquent areas. We further reported that the molecular drivers, transcriptomic abnormalities, and microenvironmental alterations akin to those found in tumors were detected in the NAT. These tumor-like molecular and microenvironmental alterations were predominantly present in the NAT within 10 mm around the tumor, despite the absence of identifiable tumor cells on rigorous histological examination. Overall, CEBR improved survival in patients with GBM in non-eloquent areas, while tumor-like alterations were present in brain tissue adjacent to the tumor. These findings provide the rationale to incorporate NAT into the extent of resection in the CEBR strategy and support further investigation of the association between its resection and patient prognosis.

title: Central neuroendocrine governance as a unifying framework for host–tumor interaction: From afferent sensing to therapeutic modulation
abstract: Cancer is not biologically confined to the tumor bed. Cachexia, fatigue, metabolic dysfunction, circadian disruption, and immune dysfunction reflect disturbances that local models alone cannot fully explain. The brain is well positioned to participate in these processes because it continuously samples circulating signals and coordinates endocrine and autonomic responses. Yet the afferent side of this communication has received less attention than its downstream consequences. Here, we synthesize evidence showing that cytokines, hormones, metabolites, and cargo carried by extracellular vesicles can engage central sensory interfaces and integrative regions, particularly circumventricular organs and hypothalamic and brainstem circuits. We use the term Endocriception to describe afferent humoral sensing and early central decoding of circulating biochemical signals, and focus here on how tumor- and host-associated changes engage this process in cancer. Central neuroendocrine governance refers to the subsequent integration of this information and the generation of autonomic and endocrine outputs. Persistent inflammation, stress, circadian disruption, and impaired feedback may gradually reconfigure this regulatory system. The resulting changes can affect systemic immunity, metabolism, behavior, and host tolerance of cancer. Evidence is strongest for a limited number of pathways, whereas many proposed links remain incomplete or dependent on tumor type and experimental context. We therefore present central neuroendocrine governance as a working framework for organizing current evidence and guiding mechanistic studies, biomarker development, and interventions aimed at restoring host physiology.

title: Corrigendum to “Chinese guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of Craniopharyngioma in children (2025)” [Cancer Lett. 659 (2026) 218784]
Tumor endothelial cells as vascular immune gatekeepers: reprogramming the vascular-immune interface for cancer immunotherapy
abstract: Despite durable clinical responses to immunotherapy in a subset of patients, most solid tumors remain refractory owing to an immune-excluded phenotype characterized by limited trafficking, infiltration, and function of effector immune cells within the tumor microenvironment (TME). Tumor endothelial cells (TECs) function as vascular immune gatekeepers that orchestrate this process. Driven by persistent pro-angiogenic signaling and metabolic stress, TECs establish a multilayered immune barrier through structurally abnormal, poorly perfused vasculature, endothelial anergy, and active immunosuppressive programs. TECs directly suppress effector T-cell and natural killer (NK)-cell function through checkpoint-like ligands, death-ligand pathways, and immunometabolic mechanisms involving adenosine production and tryptophan catabolism. Simultaneously, they recruit, retain, and reprogram immunosuppressive leukocytes, thereby reinforcing immune exclusion and therapeutic resistance. Here, we propose a TEC-centric vascular immune gatekeeping framework and review strategies to reprogram tumor vessels from immune barriers into conduits for effective immune-cell trafficking and activation. We discuss endothelial-directed monotherapies that transiently normalize or reset TEC states, together with combination strategies integrating vascular modulation with immune checkpoint blockade, adoptive and innate immune-cell therapies, cancer vaccines, oncolytic viruses, STING agonists, and multifunctional antibodies. We also highlight key translational considerations, including biomarker-guided patient stratification, pharmacodynamic monitoring using mechanism-based endpoints, and optimization of treatment dose and scheduling within the vascular normalization window. Overall, this review establishes endothelial reprogramming as a central strategy for overcoming vascular immune gatekeeping and provides a mechanistic framework for biomarker-guided vascular-immune combination therapies in solid tumors.

title: AMPK signaling in cancer: Molecular insights and therapeutic opportunities
abstract: AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) is a highly conserved serine/threonine kinase regarded as an indispensable energy sensor during metabolic stress, coordinating diverse biological processes, including glycolysis, the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, mitochondrial dynamics, and multiple stress-responsive signaling pathways. Growing evidence shows that dysregulated AMPK signaling plays closely linked roles in tumorigenesis. Depending on the context, AMPK signaling can suppress or promote tumor growth. Mechanistically, dysregulated AMPK kinase activity contributes to metabolic reprogramming, mitochondrial dysfunction, and epigenetic alterations, all recognized hallmarks of cancer. Consequently, targeting AMPK signaling has emerged as a promising strategy for cancer therapy. In this review, we summarize the molecular mechanisms regulating AMPK signaling, discuss its dual functions in tumor biology, highlight recent advances in AMPK-targeted therapeutic strategies, and address current challenges and future perspectives for the clinical translation of AMPK-targeted cancer therapy.

title: Spatial plasticity and multidirectional crosstalk of cancer-associated adipocytes in therapy-remodeled niches
abstract: Cancer-associated adipocytes (CAAs) are increasingly recognized as active and heterogeneous components of the tumor microenvironment. Initially defined as tumor-adjacent adipocytes characterized by lipid depletion, reduced expression of mature adipocyte markers, and inflammatory activation, CAAs are now understood to encompass a spectrum of context-dependent states. These states are shaped by anatomical location, preexisting adipocyte properties, tumor-derived signals, and therapeutic exposure. Through metabolic exchange, paracrine signaling, direct cell contact, extracellular-vesicle communication, and matrix remodeling, CAAs influence tumor-cell plasticity, metastatic colonization, immune dysfunction, stromal organization, and treatment response. In turn, signals from tumor, immune, and stromal cells continuously reshape adipocyte identity and function, placing CAAs within reciprocal multicellular networks. This review examines the evolving criteria used to identify CAAs, their lineage origins and plasticity, their spatial organization, and their interactions with tumor, immune, and stromal compartments. The contribution of CAAs to therapeutic adaptation is also discussed, together with potential intervention points involving CAA-derived outputs and the metabolic dependencies induced in recipient cells. Finally, major methodological challenges are considered. Adipocyte-resolved profiling, lineage tracing, spatial multiomics, lipid flux analysis, and physiologically relevant models will be needed to distinguish transient remodeling from stable state transitions and to identify context-specific therapeutic vulnerabilities.

title: Next-generation CAR-macrophage therapies: Design principles and advances in cancer treatment
abstract: Macrophages possess intrinsic tumor-homing and tissue-infiltrating abilities, performing various effector functions, including phagocytosis and antigen presentation. These properties make chimeric antigen receptor macrophages (CAR-M) a promising approach to overcoming major barriers in cellular therapy for solid tumors. This review systematically compares and critically evaluates key design variables that determine the therapeutic activity and clinical feasibility of CAR-M, including CAR architecture, macrophage source, gene-delivery method, and manufacturing strategy. We also discuss emerging engineering approaches tailored to macrophage biology, including macrophage-adapted intracellular signaling, regulation of phagocytic checkpoints, metabolic and phenotypic reprogramming, and combinations with immunomodulatory therapies. Their therapeutic potential and translational boundaries are assessed based on current preclinical evidence and early clinical findings. Notably, the major barriers to clinical translation are shifting from focusing solely on antitumor potency to addressing system-level challenges involving cell source and product consistency, in vivo expansion and persistence, phenotypic stability, off-target toxicity, and scalable manufacturing. Therefore, we propose that next-generation CAR-M development should move beyond conventional optimization of the CAR construct to multidimensional engineering centered on macrophage biology. Coordinated optimization of receptor signaling, antigen recognition, cell-state control, delivery, and safety mechanisms will be essential to balance efficacy, persistence, safety, and manufacturability. This review provides an integrated framework for the rational design and clinical evaluation of CAR-M and the development of next-generation CAR-M cellular therapy platforms.

title: CHK1/2 as a potential therapeutic target in Neurofibromatosis type 2 schwannomas
abstract: The Merlin protein, encoded by the tumor suppressor gene Neurofibromatosis type II (NF2), serves as a linker between the actin cytoskeleton, the plasma membrane receptors, and other intracellular signaling molecules. While there is a basic understanding of how Merlin regulates oncogenic signaling pathways, current targeted therapies have yet to demonstrate consistent clinical efficacy. Using a library of protein kinase inhibitors, we found that NF2-null Schwann cells (SCs) were uniquely sensitive to prexasertib, a drug that targets the DNA damage response pathway kinases CHK1/2 (Checkpoint Kinase 1 and 2). NF2-null SC proliferation was also sensitive to small molecule inhibitors of CHK1/2 downstream effectors. At baseline, NF2-null SCs have increased RAC1 activity, elevated levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, and higher levels of DNA damage. Exposing NF2-null SCs to DNA damaging agents such as doxorubicin or carboplatin, alone or in combination with prexasertib, further decreased their proliferation. Consistent with this idea, suppressing RAC1 or NOX2 activity with small molecule inhibitors, decreased ROS production and restored resistance to prexasertib in NF2-null hSCs, suggesting that active RAC1 and high ROS render NF2-null hSC uniquely vulnerable to DNA damage. Furthermore, restoring NF2 expression in NF2-null Schwann cells restored their resistance to prexasertib, reduced RAC1 activity, and lowered levels of ROS and DNA damage. The intrinsic elevation of RAC1, ROS, and DNA damage in NF2-null hSCs suggest that inhibiting DNA damage response pathways might be clinically useful in patients with NF2-null schwannomas.

title: Four clinical lenses for interpreting the Chinese guideline for pediatric craniopharyngioma
CDK9 degradation suppresses gastroesophageal cancer growth and overcomes radiation resistance through chromatin remodeling and YAP1/TEAD downregulation
abstract: Background: Gastroesophageal cancer (GEAC) remains a major health burden and urgently needs novel therapeutic targets. The inhibition of CDK9's activity holds the potential to be a highly effective anti-cancer therapeutic. However, the functional role of CDK9, and its potential targeting in GEAC, remain largely unknown. Objective: We aim to evaluate the potential of degradation CDK9 in GEAC treatment and explore its mechanisms. Design: We evaluated the expression and distribution of CDK9 in GEAC tissue. We designed and synthesized novel CDK9 degraders using proteolysis targeting chimeras (PROTACs) strategy and selected the promising one for further anti-tumor activity evaluation both in vitro and in vivo. We evaluated the effects of CDK9 degradation on epigenetic reactivation, gene expression and chromatin accessibility. We evaluated the co-targeting of CDK9 and YAP/Tead signaling for GEAC treatment, especially for radiation-resistant tumor treatment. Results: We demonstrated significantly elevated CDK9 expression in primary GEAC tumor tissues compared to normal tissues, in association with poor survival. We developed a novel CDK9 degrader, YX0597, reducing RNA Pol II Serine 2 phosphorylation, and inhibition MCL-1; this was accompanied by potent inhibition of GEAC cell growth, especially in radiation-resistant tumor cells. Mechanistically, YX0597 strongly enhanced chromatin accessibility, activating epigenetically silenced genes; and dramatically inhibited YAP/TEAD signaling. CDK9 closely interacts with YAP/TEAD signaling, and co-targeting these two mediators could be a novel treatment strategy for the treatment of GEAC. Conclusion: Our studies reveal a new avenue for targeting CDK9-hyperactivated GEAC tumors, especially in combination with YAP1/TEAD inhibition in radiation-resistant GEAC tumors. What is already known on this subject?: Gastroesophageal cancer (GEAC), the third-leading cause of global cancer death and urgently needs novel targeted therapies. Targeted protein degradation has emerged as an attractive strategy to fight cancer, complementing the activity of traditional small-molecule inhibitors. Cyclin-dependent kinase 9 (CDK9) has been implicated in various cancers. Recently, CDK9 degraders have now been developed for future clinical benefit in targeting tumors with highly activated CDK9. What are the new findings?: In this study, we show that CDK9 expression was significantly elevated in primary GEAC tumor tissues including PDXs compared to normal tissues, in association with poor survival. We developed a novel CDK9 degrader XY0597 and proved that it inhibits the progression of GEAC by increasing chromatin accessibility and down-regulating YAP/Tead signaling. We also proved a strong connection between CDK9 and YAP/TEAD signaling and Co-targeting them synergistically inhibits GEAC tumor cell growth, especially in tumors with high YAP signaling activity, such as radiation-resistant cancer. How might it impact on clinical practice in the foreseeable future?: Our data suggests that CDK9 is a viable anticancer target in GEAC. We demonstrate that a novel CDK9 degrader, YX0597, has high potential clinical application for GEAC treatment, especially in radiation-resistant cancer. We reveal the crosstalk of CDK9 and YAP/TEAD signaling, and that co-targeting these two mediators could be a new avenue for targeting CDK9-hyperactivated GEAC primary and radiation-resistant tumors.

title: LRH-1 is a novel regulator of neutrophil-driven immune responses within the tumor microenvironment
abstract: Abstract Elevated plasma cholesterol levels have been linked to worse outcomes in breast and ovarian cancer. Prior work including our own has demonstrated that myeloid immune cells are highly responsive to cholesterol fluctuations and to proteins involved in cholesterol regulation. However, the specific roles of Liver Receptor Homolog-1 (LRH-1, or NR5A2), a key transcriptional regulator of cholesterol homeostasis, within myeloid cells remains largely undefined. Interestingly, LRH-1 mRNA levels are reduced in both breast and ovarian tumors compared to normal tissue. Its elevated expression within tumors is associated with increased survival time. These clinical correlations prompted us to explore the role of LRH-1 in myeloid cells particularly in the context of breast and ovarian cancer progression. Initial analyses confirmed LRH-1 expression in various myeloid cell types, with particularly high levels in neutrophils. We therefore focused on how LRH-1 influences neutrophil behaviors relevant to cancer, including migration, NETosis, phagocytosis, and interactions with T cells. Small molecule ligands for LRH-1 regulated neutrophil migration towards cancer cells. Phagocytosis was also regulated by LRH-1 small molecule ligands, the extent being dependent on type of bait ( e. coli vs. cancer cells). In T cell co-cultures, neutrophils pretreated with an LRH-1 agonist promoted greater T cell expansion - particularly in CD4⁺ cells - while LRH-1 inhibition suppressed this response. Moreover, LRH-1 activation reduced NETosis, while treatment with an antagonist or inverse agonist enhanced NETosis. Treatment of mice with an inverse agonist of LRH-1 increased the growth of 4T1 and E0771 mammary tumors. Given prior evidence that neutrophils contribute to the recurrence of dormant lesions, we further examined the role of LRH-1 in this context. Mice harboring dormant D2.0R mammary cancer lesions treated with an LRH-1 inverse agonist exhibited earlier tumor recurrence and enhanced metastatic progression compared to vehicle-treated controls. In contrast, treatment with BL001, a small chemical LRH-1 agonist, delayed recurrence in D2.0R-grafted mice. Collectively, these findings reveal that LRH-1 is a novel regulator of neutrophil-driven immune responses within the tumor microenvironment. LRH-1 thus remerges as a promising therapeutic target to suppress metastasis or prevent recurrence in breast cancer.

title: Early transcriptional divergence and spatial remodeling toward immune activation and evasion shape lung adenocarcinoma precancer evolution
abstract: Tumor heterogeneity is a universal feature of cancer and may arise as early as precancer stages during lung adenocarcinoma evolution, yet the emergence of aggressive transcriptional programs remains incompletely understood. Here, we integrated spatial transcriptomics with single-cell RNA sequencing to characterize inter- and intratumoral heterogeneity across hyperplasia, adenoma, and invasive adenocarcinoma (IAC) in a genetically engineered mouse model (129S4/Sv Kras LSL-G12D/+ ). Disease progression was accompanied by coordinated remodeling of epithelial, stromal, and immune compartments, along with dynamic changes in proliferation, immune response, and metabolic pathways. Notably, lesions of the same histological stage exhibited substantial transcriptional heterogeneity. By quantifying dedifferentiation states, we identified a subset of adenomas that had already diverged toward highly proliferative and metabolically active programs despite lacking invasive features. These lesions were further marked by early chromosome 6 amplification, whose corresponding human ortholog signature recapitulated aggressive proliferation-associated programs in early-stage human lung adenocarcinoma. Spatial analyses further revealed pronounced intratumoral heterogeneity within IAC, with tumor core regions showing increased proliferation and metabolism but reduced immune signaling compared to peripheral regions. In addition, immune checkpoint gene expression in T cells was transiently elevated at the hyperplasia stage, suggesting early immune modulation prior to overt malignancy. Together, these findings indicate that aggressive transcriptional divergence can emerge early during lung adenocarcinoma evolution and that spatial organization critically shapes tumor and immune programs before and after invasion.

title: UBL3 modification reduces nuclear POLE levels to potentiate antitumor immunity in aero-upper digestive squamous cell carcinomas
abstract: While immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have revolutionized treatment of the patients with aero-upper digestive squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs), including esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) and lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC), only a subset of patients benefit from ICIs, therefore entailing exploration of the mechanisms to regulate treatment responsiveness. POLE, as a subunit of DNA polymerase ε, possesses 3'-5' proofreading activity, and its mutations have been associated with favourable response to ICIs in several solid tumors. However, post-translational modification (PTM) of POLE and its impact on the therapeutic efficacy of ICIs are unknown. Here, this study demonstrates that ubiquitin-like protein 3 (Ubl3), whose expression is markedly downregulated in SCCs, covalently binds to Pole, reduces nuclear Pole levels, triggers DNA damage, and activates cGAS-STING signaling pathway. Notably, Ubl3 modification of Pole significantly primes the local immune microenvironment to mitigate the growth of murine aero-upper digestive SCC cells and boost the efficacy of αPD-1 treatment in vivo. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis further revealed that UBL3 expression is positively correlated with better clinical outcomes in a cohort of ESCC patients receiving neoadjuvant chemotherapy combined with αPD-1. Together, our findings unravel UBL3 modification as a novel PTM mechanism governing subcellular location of POLE and its influence on immunotherapy responsiveness, thus making UBL3 modification as a promising immunomodulatory approach to enhance immunotherapy efficacy in patients with aero-upper digestive SCCs.

title: Extracellular vesicle–mediated strategies for cancer tissue normalisation
abstract: Tissue normalisation has emerged as an interesting therapeutic concept in oncology, aiming to correct the structural, metabolic, and immunological tissue abnormalities that enable tumour progression and treatment resistance. Rather than targeting cancer cells directly, this approach aims to re-establish homeostatic tissue architecture, immune surveillance, and metabolic balance. Interventions that target stromal components, such as cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), immune cells, or stiffness of extracellular matrix (ECM), have been shown to shift tumour cells toward a less aggressive state, underscoring the plasticity of cancer cells and the importance of their interactions with the microenvironment. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are increasingly recognised as both contributors to tissue dysfunction in tumours and promising tools for restoring tissue homeostasis. EVs circulate across most biofluids and can cross biological barriers to reach distant tissues. They naturally carry nucleic acids, including regulatory miRNAs, along with proteins, lipids, and metabolites that influence cell behaviour, making them attractive tools for tissue normalisation. Moreover, engineered EVs could be designed to deliver targeted "normalisation signals" and hold strong clinical potential as next-generation delivery systems. Here, we explore how EVs, whether native or engineered, can intervene in key tumour-driving processes, including senescence, fibrosis, inflammation, and immune evasion, to shift the microenvironment toward a normalised, less malignant state.

title: Targeting CDC7 overcomes gemcitabine resistance in cholangiocarcinoma by inducing cellular senescence
abstract: Advanced-stage cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) frequently develops resistance to chemotherapy, highlighting an urgent unmet need for novel therapeutic strategies. Here, we analyzed 16 pairs of CCA and adjacent non-tumor tissues, and demonstrated that dysregulation of the cell cycle machinery is a hallmark of CCA, closely associated with chemoresistance and poor prognosis. Targeting aberrant cell cycle regulation therefore represents a promising approach to improve current treatment outcomes. We identify the CDC7 inhibitor XL413 as an effective agent capable of re-sensitizing gemcitabine-resistant tumors across multiple preclinical models of CCA. Mechanistic analyses, including transcriptomic profiling, reveal that combination therapy activates senescence-associated pathways, with therapeutic efficacy is mediated via a ROS-DNA damage-senescence cascade. Notably, synergistic induction of cellular senescence is observed in CCA cells upon co-treatment with a CDC7 inhibitor and gemcitabine. Collectively, these findings provide robust preclinical evidence supporting the combination of gemcitabine and CDC7 inhibitors as a viable therapeutic strategy to enhance the clinical management of CCA.

title: Oncogenic circPRRC2B regulates redox homeostasis via stabilizing TALDO1 protein of the pentose phosphate pathway in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma
abstract: It remains largely unclear whether oncogenic super-enhancers (SEs) can drive expression of circular RNAs (circRNAs). In this study, we for the first time profiled the comprehensive circRNA landscapes of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) after suppressing genome-wide SE activities. We identified a novel SE-driven circPRRC2B, as the product of back-splicing of exons 2, 3, 4 and 5 of PRRC2B pre-mRNA, which was controlled by RNA binding protein HuR. Indeed, SE drives high levels of PRRC2B transcription, promotes production of PRRC2B pre-mRNAs, boosts back-splicing of PRRC2B pre-mRNAs, and elevates circPRRC2B expression. ETS1 acts as a key transcriptional factor in SE-driven PRRC2B transcription and circPRRC2B biogenesis. Interestingly, circPRRC2B, but not PRRC2B, could promote proliferation, invasion and metastasis of ESCC in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, circPRRC2B binds to TALDO1 and enhances BAP1-mediated TALDO1 de-ubiquitination in ESCC cells. Therefore, circPRRC2B stabilizes and sustains high expression of TALDO1, activates the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP), elevates the glutathione levels via supplying more NADPH via the PPP, inhibits production of reactive oxygen species in mitochondrion, maintains cellular redox equilibrium, and, thus, leads to cancer progression. Importantly, we developed antisense oligonucleotides targeting circPRRC2B which exhibited remarkable inhibition of ESCC growth. Our findings highlighted circPRRC2B as a key target preserving the PPP metabolic flux and redox homeostasis of malignant cells, thereby offering insight into developing novel therapeutics for cancers.

title: Fenofibrate enhances systemic antitumor efficacy of high- and low-dose radiotherapy plus PD-1 blockade through CD8+ T-cell metabolic reprogramming and LDRT tumor conditioning
abstract: Radiotherapy (RT) combined with PD-1/PD-L1 blockade can induce systemic antitumor responses, but robust control of distant lesions remains uncommon. We identified a quadruple regimen combining immunogenic hypofractionated RT (hRT; 8 Gy × 3) to the primary tumor, low-dose RT (LDRT; 3 Gy × 3) to the secondary tumor, anti–PD-1 (αPD-1), and fenofibrate (FFB), a clinically approved PPARα agonist, that enhanced antitumor efficacy in two bilateral tumor models. Only this regimen substantially improved secondary-tumor control, eradicating LDRT-treated secondary tumors in all mice in the immunologically cold C51 model and inducing prolonged control in the aggressive, αPD-1-poorly responsive B16-CD133 model. This effect required CD8 + T cells. Tumor-specific CD8 + TILs showed enhanced effector function, reduced exhaustion, increased mitochondrial fitness, and a shift toward mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation (FAO), with scRNA-seq supporting PPARα/FAO-associated remodeling, including upregulation of Cpt1a , encoding the FAO enzyme CPT1A, in effector-associated, proliferative, and clonally expanded subsets. Both antitumor efficacy and T-cell metabolic remodeling were reversed by the CPT1 inhibitor etomoxir. By contrast, LDRT impaired tumor-cell mitochondrial fitness, while FFB shifted tumor cells from FAO toward glycolytic reliance and induced only slight apoptosis. Consistently, in vivo data argued against direct LDRT-mediated tumor-cell debulking. The quadruple regimen increased vascular MECA-79 expression, while LDRT enhanced endothelial ICAM-1/VCAM-1 and tumor-cell CXCL9/CXCL10 expression in secondary tumors, consistent with local conditioning favoring T-cell recruitment. These findings highlight FFB as a clinically tractable metabolic modulator and link FFB-enhanced hRT/LDRT/αPD-1-induced systemic antitumor efficacy to metabolic reprogramming of tumor-specific CD8 + TILs and conditioning of the LDRT-treated tumor microenvironment.

title: Early WEE1 inhibition prevents senescence-like epigenetic reprogramming of pioneer TMZ-resistant cells and synergizes with temozolomide in MYC-high glioblastoma
abstract: In proliferative glioblastoma, a subset of tumor cells survives early temozolomide (TMZ) exposure and drives eventual-resistance, yet the underlying mechanism remains unclear. We found that MYC target activation was associated with attenuated TMZ survival benefit in CGGA cohorts. In patient-derived MYC-high glioma cells, TMZ increased apoptosis but left a larger residual viable population due to enhanced proliferation; we defined these surviving cells as pioneer resistant (P-R) cells, which exhibited reduced TMZ sensitivity and a competitive survival advantage. Mechanistically, P-R cells adopted a senescence-like state via two coordinated arms of chromatin remodeling. On one hand, H3K27ac-dependent super-enhancers were gained at senescence-associated secretory genes; the CBP/p300 inhibitor A485 reverted the senescence-like state and restored TMZ cytotoxicity; On another hand, chromatin closed, reducing MYC occupancy at cell-cycle genes despite unchanged MYC protein, and suppressed nascent transcription and m 6 A modification, accompanied by cell-cycle arrest in some P-R cells. Furthermore, time-course analysis revealed that chromatin closure at cell-cycle genes is likely a temporally ordered epigenetic remodeling process, initiated by DNA damage-associated G2/M arrest mediated by WEE1 activation, followed by γH2AX-mediated recruitment of SUV39H1, which deposits H3K9me3 at MYC-bound loci to close chromatin. Functionally, early, but not delayed, inhibition of WEE1 with the novel brain-penetrant inhibitor TSL2304 blocked senescence-like epigenetic reprogramming, synergized with TMZ in vitro, and significantly prolonged survival in an orthotopic glioblastoma model. Together, these findings reveal a temporally ordered epigenetic remodeling in MYC-high glioblastoma that promotes survival after early TMZ exposure, and identify early WEE1 inhibition as a strategy to synergize with TMZ.

title: Editorial Board
Erianin targets glutathione reductase to trigger immunogenic cell death and sensitize pancreatic cancer to PD-1 blockade
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) responds poorly to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB), largely because of its immunosuppressive and T-cell-excluded tumor microenvironment. While inducing immunogenic cell death (ICD) offers a promising strategy to enhance tumor immunogenicity, redox-targeted ICD inducers with defined molecular targets remain limited in PDAC. Here, a functional screen of natural compounds identified erianin as a potent ICD inducer in PDAC. Erianin triggered canonical ICD hallmarks, including cell-surface calreticulin exposure, extracellular release of HMGB1 and ATP, thereby promoting dendritic-cell maturation, antigen cross-presentation and CD8 + T-cell activation. Target-engagement assays together with genetic perturbation supported glutathione reductase (GSR) as a functionally important erianin target. Erianin decreased the GSH/GSSG ratio, accompanied by increased oxidative stress and preferential activation of the PERK-eIF2α-ATF4-CHOP branch of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress response. Mutational and rescue experiments identified ARG-233 as an important residue required for GSR-dependent protection against erianin-induced redox stress and ICD. In syngeneic PDAC models, erianin-treated tumor cells elicited protective antitumor immunity in a tumor-challenge setting, while a therapeutic regimen combining erianin with anti-PD-1 antibody suppressed tumor growth and was associated with increased dendritic-cell activation and enhanced cytotoxic CD8 + T-cell infiltration. These findings define a GSR-associated redox-immune axis that links glutathione metabolism to immunogenic ER stress and provide a rationale for combining erianin with PD-1 blockade in immunologically cold PDAC.

title: MUC16 drives macrophage-mediated immunosuppression in pancreatic cancer
abstract: Mucin-16 (MUC16) is overexpressed in >60% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cases and correlates with poor outcomes, yet its role in regulating tumor-immune interactions remains incompletely defined. Using KPC and KPC-MUC16 knockout (KPC-MUC16 KO ) genetically engineered and orthotopic mouse models, we show that loss of MUC16 markedly reduces tumor burden and reprograms the tumor microenvironment (TME) toward a less immunosuppressive state. MUC16 deficiency significantly decreased CD206 + and Ym1/2 + M2-like macrophages, increased the M1/M2 ratio, and improved survival. Cytokine profiling identified CCL2 and Serpin-E1 as MUC16- dependent secreted factors that promote macrophage recruitment and polarization; neutralization of these cytokines reduced macrophage migration in vitro. Bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDM) exposed to MUC16-expressing tumor cells or conditioned media adopted a CD206 + Arg1 + M2-like phenotype, whereas MUC16 KO tumor signals favored inflammatory CD86 + iNOS + M1-like polarization. Macrophage depletion using clodronate liposomes significantly impaired tumor growth in MUC16-competent tumors but had minimal effect in KPC-MUC16 KO tumors, indicating dependence on macrophage-mediated immunosuppression in the former group. Spatial transcriptomics revealed a globally distinct TME in MUC16 KO tumors, including enhanced antigen-presentation programs, increased complement activation, and fibroblast states skewed toward pro-inflammatory signaling. These findings establish MUC16 as a key orchestrator of macrophage-driven immunosuppression in PDAC and support therapeutic strategies combining MUC16-targeted interventions with TME-reprogramming approaches.

title: Lactate-induced PPP1R1B upregulation drives resistance to neoadjuvant immunotherapy in NSCLC via IRF3 dephosphorylation
abstract: Neoadjuvant immunotherapy has improved clinical outcomes in resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC); however, a substantial proportion of patients fail to achieve durable responses, and the mechanisms underlying therapeutic resistance remain incompletely understood. Here, we identified protein phosphatase 1 regulatory inhibitor subunit 1B (PPP1R1B) as a metabolic driver of immunotherapy resistance in NSCLC through RNA sequencing of tumors with differential responses to neoadjuvant anti-PD-1 therapy. PPP1R1B was significantly upregulated in non-responders and correlated with poor prognosis in NSCLC patients. Mechanistically, PPP1R1B directly interacted with IRF3 through the Arg29 residue and promoted dephosphorylation of IRF3 at Ser396, thereby suppressing IRF3 activation and downstream interferon-β (IFN-β) signaling. PPP1R1B-mediated inhibition of IFN-β signaling reduced CD8 + T-cell infiltration and impaired antitumor immunity, ultimately conferring resistance to anti-PD-1 therapy in vivo. Blockade of IFN-β signaling abrogated the antitumor effects induced by PPP1R1B depletion, supporting an immune-dependent mechanism. Notably, tumors resistant to neoadjuvant immunotherapy exhibited impaired oxidative phosphorylation and excessive lactate accumulation. Lactate induced PPP1R1B expression through NF-κB-dependent transcriptional activation, linking metabolic reprogramming to innate immune suppression. Collectively, our findings identify a lactate/NF-κB/PPP1R1B/IRF3 signaling axis that drives immune evasion and resistance to neoadjuvant immunotherapy in NSCLC, and nominate PPP1R1B as a potential biomarker and therapeutic target for overcoming anti-PD-1 resistance.

title: Acquisition of Therapeutic Resistance and Structured Tissue Differentiation via Activation of the Life Cycle of Polyploid Giant Cancer Cells
abstract: To elucidate the mechanisms underlying therapy-induced resistance, we investigated the temporal dynamics of the polyploid giant cancer cell (PGCC) life cycle following treatment with the microtubule-destabilizing agent vincristine (VCR). Longitudinal live-cell fluorescence imaging revealed that VCR-induced mitotic suppression activated a distinct PGCC life cycle characterized by nuclear amplification and progressive cellular reprogramming. At the cellular level, PGCCs entered a senescence-like state accompanied by an enhanced senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), increased epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), acquisition of early embryonic-like features, and multilineage differentiation potential into ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. PGCC-derived progeny exhibited dose- and time-dependent changes in proliferative behavior, aggressive phenotypes in vitro, along with time-dependent tumorigenic potential in vivo. Remarkably, at the tissue level, PGCCs also underwent spatial nuclear reorganization and self-organization into morphologically defined glandular epithelial structures exhibiting varying degrees of tissue maturation, reminiscent of early embryonic development. Silencing IL1β, IL6, or IL8, or pharmacologically inhibiting their receptors, suppressed PGCC formation, budding, EMT, and embryonic-like reprogramming associated with tissue morphogenesis. Furthermore, NAMPT emerged as a key regulator of embryonic-like stemness, glandular morphogenesis, and structural expansion. Together, these findings reveal that therapeutic stress activates a PGCC life cycle capable of generating two divergent outcomes: resistant tumor regeneration through clonal selection of undifferentiated tumor cells and organized tissue differentiation through spatial nuclear reprogramming. Our study establishes a conceptual framework linking therapy-induced polyploidization, developmental plasticity, and resistance generation at both cellular and tissue levels.

title: Combination of canagliflozin and adagrasib as a novel targeted therapy for LKB1-KRASG12C co-mutated NSCLC
abstract: In recent years, significant progress has been made in developing targeted therapy for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, these therapies are only applicable to specific NSCLC groups with corresponding gene mutations. Therefore, developing novel targeted therapies to benefit more patients remains an important task. Our prior work demonstrated that LKB1-mutant NSCLC cells are highly susceptible to cell death induced by glucose starvation. In this study, we investigated a novel combinational therapeutic strategy utilizing a sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor canagliflozin and a covalent KRAS G12C inhibitor adagrasib, two clinically approved therapeutics, to selectively target LKB1-KRAS G12C co-mutated NSCLC. First, we verified the co-occurrence of LKB1 and KRAS mutations in clinical NSCLC cohorts. Second, compared to other SGLT2 inhibitors, canagliflozin induced higher cytotoxicity in LKB1-mutant cells, and SGLT2 knockdown partially attenuated this effect. Mechanistically, the high susceptibility to canagliflozin was associated with impaired activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK). Furthermore, canagliflozin suppressed mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) activity and robustly inhibited cell growth in LKB1-mutant models in vitro. Third, adagrasib exhibited selective cytotoxicity in KRAS G12C -mutated NSCLC. Finally, the combination of canagliflozin and adagrasib synergistically reduced cell viability in LKB1-KRAS G12C co-mutated H23 and H2122 cells in vitro. Importantly, canagliflozin attenuated the adaptive MAPK signaling rebound induced by adagrasib in vitro. The therapeutic potential of this combination was confirmed in an H2122 nude mouse xenograft model in vivo. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that a combination of canagliflozin and adagrasib suppresses LKB1-KRAS G12C co-mutated NSCLC, laying a solid preclinical foundation for developing a new therapeutic strategy for this group of NSCLC.

title: Immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy in COPD-concomitant lung cancer: A review of efficacy outcomes and mechanistic insights
abstract: The coexistence of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and lung cancer (LC) presents a complex clinical scenario with distinct pathological interactions. Beyond shared epidemiological and genetic risk factors, COPD reshapes the pulmonary immune microenvironment through reprogrammed immune-cell compartments, aberrant programmed cell death, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), fostering an immunologically "hot" but pathologically permissive milieu that simultaneously drives carcinogenesis and influences treatment responsiveness. Recent evidence suggests that COPD may confer an altered immunological microenvironment that paradoxically enhances responsiveness to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in patients with LC. This review mainly synthesizes clinical evidence on the efficacy of ICI, currently the most widely used immunotherapy, in LC patients concomitant with COPD and elucidates potential immunological and molecular mechanisms underlying observed clinical benefits, including heightened programmed cell death protein ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression, elevated tumor mutational burden, increased human leukocyte antigen I (HLA-I) expression, enriched tissue-resident memory T cells and mucosal-associated invariant T cells, and a macrophage polarization shift toward a pro-inflammatory phenotype, with benefits appearing largely attributable to patients with mild-to-moderate airflow obstruction. The safety profile of ICIs in this population-exacerbation risk, eosinophilic airway disease, checkpoint inhibitor pneumonitis (CIP), and autoimmune thyroiditis-is appraised, alongside emerging strategies such as lymphocyte-activation gene 3 (LAG-3), T-cell immunoglobulin and mucin-domain containing-3 (TIM-3), and T cell immunoreceptor with Ig and ITIM domains (TIGIT) blockade and the immunomodulatory potential of COPD medications (inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting β-agonists). Current evidence remains limited by small retrospective cohorts and heterogeneous stratification. Large-scale prospective studies are warranted. This review aims to clarify the prognostic value of concomitant COPD and guide precision therapeutic strategies for this growing comorbid population.

title: Saturation mutagenesis library screening identifies on-target secondary resistance mutations in KRASG12D-selective inhibitors
abstract: KRAS is the most frequently mutated oncogene in pancreatic cancer, with over 90% of patients harboring KRAS mutations, approximately 45% of which are G12D substitutions. The development of KRAS G12D selective inhibitors, such as HRS-4642, MRTX1133 and RMC-9805, has brought new hope for treating this patient population. However, the clinical efficacy of these inhibitors is limited by the emergence of acquired resistance, the mechanisms of which remain incompletely understood. Our study employed a KRAS saturation mutagenesis library to systematically map the landscape of KRAS mutations conferring resistance to HRS-4642 and MRTX1133. We identified several secondary mutations-including R73P, E63P, D69W, and M72K-that confer resistance to both inhibitors, while M72H was found specifically resistant to HRS-4642. We further characterized the impact of these mutations on KRAS downstream signaling and performed structural modeling of the mutant proteins. Through molecular dynamics simulations, we suggested that the R73P mutation, although distant from the binding pocket, is predicted to exert a global dynamic effect on the allosteric site, thereby disrupting inhibitor-protein interactions. This suggests the existence of a novel class of KRAS resistance mutations and a previously unrecognized mechanism of acquired resistance to KRAS-targeted therapies. Furthermore, we identified Y64W, A59G, and R73P as mutations that concurrently confer resistance to the tri-complex inhibitor RMC-9805, as well as to the allosteric inhibitors MRTX1133 and HRS-4642. This comprehensive analysis delineates the global landscape of secondary resistance mutations to KRAS G12D -selective inhibitors.

title: Reprogramming Muscle Proteostasis in Cancer Cachexia: Transcriptional Mechanisms and Therapeutic Opportunities
abstract: Cancer cachexia is a multifactorial syndrome characterized by progressive skeletal muscle wasting that diminishes quality of life, limits responses to anticancer therapies, and increases mortality. Although excessive protein degradation has traditionally been viewed as a primary driver of muscle loss, cachectic muscle undergoes broader disruption of proteostasis involving protein turnover, organelle quality control, stress adaptation, metabolism, and regenerative capacity. Accumulating evidence suggests that diverse tumor- and host-derived signals converge on interconnected transcriptional networks that coordinate these processes. Rather than functioning independently, transcription factors integrate inflammatory, metabolic, hormonal, and cellular-stress signals to generate catabolic, stress-responsive, anabolic, and regenerative programs whose effects vary with disease stage and cellular context. Importantly, these transcriptional responses are not uniformly pathological but can represent causal, adaptive, or compensatory programs. Epigenetic, post-transcriptional, and post-translational mechanisms provide additional layers that shape the activation and magnitude of these transcriptional programs. Emerging single-cell and multi-omic approaches have further revealed myofiber- and cell-specific regulatory networks underlying the heterogeneous response of skeletal muscle to tumor growth. In this review, we argue that transcriptional reprogramming represents a central integrative mechanism through which diverse catabolic signals remodel skeletal muscle proteostasis, and we examine how network-level regulation contributes to muscle adaptation and wasting in cancer cachexia. Defining which regulatory programs are causal, compensatory, or maladaptive may reveal more precise biomarkers and therapeutic targets for preserving skeletal muscle mass and function in patients with cachectic cancer.

title: Recent advances and future directions in targeting MYCN: From undruggable to druggable
abstract: MYCN is a member of the MYC family of transcription factors and a potent oncogenic driver across neural crest, neuroectodermal, and neuroendocrine malignancies, including neuroblastoma, where MYCN amplification remains one of the most powerful molecular predictors of treatment failure and poor survival. MYCN has long been considered an ideal therapeutic target, given its restricted expression in postnatal tissues and potent oncogenic activity. However, direct and selective MYCN targeting therapies have yet to be established and translated into the clinic. This reflects the challenges of drugging MYC family proteins, which lack enzymatic active sites and defined binding pockets targeted by conventional small molecules. Here, we examine the landscape of MYCN targeting strategies, from direct approaches such as MYC-MAX dimerization inhibitors to indirect approaches targeting MYCN expression, its interactors, and downstream oncogenic dependencies. We also highlight the potential of targeted protein degrader technology for directly and selectively depleting MYCN protein. We further discuss the profound immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment characteristic of MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma and the therapeutic vulnerabilities this creates. Together, these advances in understanding and technology present a renewed opportunity to translate four decades of MYCN biology into effective therapies to improve outcomes for patients with neuroblastoma and other MYCN-driven cancers.
